chapter 03 · agent

The loop, and why tools are just text

An LLM cannot do anything. It reads text and emits text — that was the whole of chapters 00 and 01, and nothing in this chapter changes it. An agent is what you get when ordinary code reads that text, acts on the world, and writes what happened back into the conversation. The model gained no new powers. It acquired a correspondent.

Two halves, in order: §1–§3 the framework — what an agent is made of, what actually crosses the wire, and what the design costs you. Then §4–§6 the build — eighty lines of real code, the five things that break, and when to stop hand-rolling.

01

The framework

Four parts and a loop. Learn where the boundary falls and the rest follows.

An agent is not a kind of model. It is an architecture you build around a model, out of four parts:

PartWhat it isWho owns it
ModelProposes the next action. Given the transcript so far, emits either an answer or a request to use a tool.the API
ToolsThe only way to touch anything. A name, a description, a JSON schema — and a function you wrote.you
EnvironmentWhatever the tools reach: a filesystem, a database, a cluster, an HTTP API, a genome.the world
ContextThe transcript. The agent's entire memory — re-read in full on every single step.you
The loopCalls the model, executes what it asked for, appends the result, calls again. Halts on a condition you choose.you

Three of the five are yours. That is the first useful thing to notice: most of an agent is ordinary software, and most agent bugs are ordinary software bugs sitting in an unfamiliar place.

The model never calls anything. This is the same argument as the END token in chapter 00, and it is worth saying in the same blunt way: a transformer is a function that returns a vector of numbers. It cannot open a file, run a job, or reach a server. What it can do is make the tokens describing a request likely — and something else acts on them:

resp = client.messages.create(...)          # the model's entire contribution
if resp.stop_reason == "tool_use":           # ← this line is the "calling".
    result = my_function(block.input)        #   It is not inside the model.

Every property that follows — that an agent can be interrupted, sandboxed, made to ask permission, or stopped dead — exists because the decision to execute lives in your process, not in the weights.

So an agent is a correspondence between a model that can only write and a loop that can only act. Next: what the letters look like.

02

What actually crosses the wire

One endpoint, four blocks, one stop reason. There is no agent API.

Everything goes through a single call — POST /v1/messages. "Tool use" is not a separate endpoint or a plugin system; it is two extra block types and one extra stop reason.

1 · You declare what exists

A tool is a name, a description, and a JSON Schema. Note what is not there: any code. You are describing a capability to a reader, not registering a function.

tools = [{
    "name": "kb_search",
    "description": "Search the paper corpus. Returns matching paper IDs and titles. "
                   "Use for questions about what the literature says.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"query": {"type": "string", "description": "search terms"}},
        "required": ["query"],
    },
}]

The description is prompt, not documentation. It is the only thing the model knows about your tool, and it is read on every step. A vague description is a bug with no stack trace — the tool simply gets called at the wrong times, or never. Write it for a competent colleague who has never seen your codebase, and say when to use it, not only what it does.

2 · The model replies with a request

When it wants the tool, the response's stop_reason is tool_use and its content carries a tool_use block beside any ordinary text:

{"role": "assistant", "content": [
   {"type": "text", "text": "I'll search the corpus first."},
   {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01A...", "name": "kb_search",
    "input": {"query": "loop extrusion CTCF"}}
]}

The input has been validated against your schema. The id is the correspondence token — your reply must quote it.

3 · You execute, and write back as the user

This is the step people find strange, and it is the most important one:

{"role": "user", "content": [
   {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01A...",
    "content": "3 papers: Rao 2014; Fudenberg 2016; Nora 2017"}
]}

A tool result is not a function return — it is a message you wrote, in the user's voice. The model does not observe your program; it reads a transcript in which something appeared claiming to be an observation. Three consequences follow immediately, and they run through the whole rest of the course:

  • You choose what it sees. Ten thousand rows or a five-line summary — the model has no way to ask for the other one. This is chapter 04's entire subject.
  • You can lie, and so can the environment. Text arriving from a tool has exactly the authority of text arriving from a user, which is why untrusted tool output is a prompt-injection surface rather than a data type.
  • Errors are content, not exceptions. A failure is a result too — see §5.

4 · The stop reason drives the loop

stop_reasonMeansYour loop should
tool_useit asked for one or more toolsexecute them, append results, call again
end_turnit is finishedbreak — this is the halt
max_tokensthe reply was cut off mid-thoughtretry or raise. Never treat as done
pause_turna server-side tool hit an iteration limitsend the turn back to continue it
refusalthe request was declinedcheck before reading content; handle or fall back

A loop that only tests tool_use and treats everything else as success will one day report a truncated answer as a finished job. That is the single most common silent bug in a hand-rolled agent.

03

What the design costs

You trade a DAG for a search. Know what you gave up.

You have written pipelines for years. An agent is a pipeline driver whose next step is chosen at run time by a model instead of by a graph you wrote in advance. Everything hard about agents falls out of that one substitution.

Workflow / DAGAgent
Who picks the next stepyou, at authoring timethe model, at run time
Same input twicesame pathpossibly a different path
Reasoning about a runread the coderead the transcript — after it ran
Handles the case you didn't foreseenosometimes — that is what you are buying
Costone passN model calls, N unpredictable
How you know it workstestsevals — chapter 07

Default to a workflow. Reach for an agent when the search is genuinely open-ended — when you cannot enumerate the branches, and a wrong branch is cheap to detect and retry. If you can draw the DAG, draw the DAG.

The four shapes, before you pick one

"Build an agent" is four different decisions, separated by two questions: who supplies the harness (the loop and its context management), and who supplies the deployment (the machine it runs on).

ShapeYou writeHarness / deploymentReach for it when
Manual loop
Messages API		the loop itselfyou build bothlearning it, or you need control no helper exposes
Tool Runner
client.beta.messages.tool_runner		just the tool functionsSDK loops; you hostcustom tools, no desire to hand-write the loop
Managed Agentsa confighosted: bothyou want the sandbox hosted too
Claude Agent SDK
claude-agent-sdk		a prompt + optionsfull harness + built-in file/bash tools; you hostyou want a batteries-included agent on your own machine

The middle two are the pair most often confused, and they are different packages. The difference is scope of harness: the Tool Runner loops over tools you define; the Agent SDK ships a filesystem-and-bash agent already built.

The deployment column decides more than the harness column. A hosted sandbox cannot reach a machine it has no route to — an internal cluster, a box behind ssh, a disk holding data that is not allowed to leave. When the compute and the data already live somewhere, the agent has to run where the data is, and three of the four shapes become one. Check this before comparing features; it usually eliminates most of the menu.

04

The eighty-line agent

The whole thing. No framework, nothing hidden.

Here is a complete, working agent. Read it once as prose — it is a while loop with one API call in it.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# ── 1. what exists ─────────────────────────────────────────
TOOLS = [{
    "name": "kb_search",
    "description": "Search the paper corpus by keyword. Returns paper IDs and "
                   "titles. Use whenever the question is about what the "
                   "literature says; do not answer from memory.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["query"],
    },
}]

def execute(name, args):
    # your actual code. Returns a STRING the model will read.
    if name == "kb_search":
        return kb_search(args["query"])
    raise KeyError(name)

# ── 2. the loop ────────────────────────────────────────────
def run(goal, max_steps=20):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]

    for step in range(max_steps):                  # never `while True`
        resp = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5",
            max_tokens=16000,
            tools=TOOLS,
            messages=messages,
        )

        if resp.stop_reason == "end_turn":         # ← the halt
            return "".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")

        if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":          # max_tokens, refusal…
            raise RuntimeError(f"unexpected stop: {resp.stop_reason}")

        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})

        results = []                                # ALL of them, one message
        for b in resp.content:
            if b.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            try:
                out = execute(b.name, b.input)
                results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                                "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": str(out)})
            except Exception as e:                  # failure is data
                results.append({"type": "tool_result",
                                "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": f"error: {e}",
                                "is_error": True})

        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

    raise RuntimeError(f"no answer in {max_steps} steps")

That is an agent. Five of those lines are the interesting ones:

LineWhy it is there
for step in range(max_steps)A model that keeps asking for tools loops forever. The bound is not optional — it is the difference between a bug and a bill.
if stop_reason == "end_turn"The halt lives in your code, exactly as in chapter 00. The model only makes stopping likely.
messages.append(assistant)Append the whole resp.content, not the text. Drop the tool_use blocks and your next request is malformed.
results = [] … one appendOne reply can contain several tool_use blocks. All results go back in one user message (§5).
is_error: TrueLet the model see the failure and try something else. An exception that escapes the loop ends the run; an error handed back is a chance to recover.
05

The five things that break

Each fails quietly. None raises where the bug is.
SymptomCauseFix
The agent stops using a tool it used happily beforeResults for parallel calls were split across several user messagesReturn every tool_result for one assistant turn in a single user message — splitting them teaches the model to stop calling in parallel
400 on the next requestA tool_use block with no matching result, or a mismatched tool_use_idEvery tool_use gets exactly one tool_result, quoting its id — including the ones that failed
A truncated answer reported as successOnly tool_use was tested; max_tokens fell through the elseBranch on every stop_reason (§2). Treat the unknown ones as errors
The tool is called at absurd moments, or neverThe description is documentation, not instructionSay when to use it and when not to. It is the only thing the model knows
Reasoning degrades as the run goes onTool output floods the context — the transcript is re-read in full every stepShape what you return: summarize, paginate, or hand back a path instead of contents → chapter 04

Parse tool inputs, never string-match them. b.input is already a parsed object — use it as one. JSON string escaping in tool arguments varies (Unicode, forward slashes), so any code that matches on a serialized form will work in testing and fail in production on the first unusual character.

06

When to stop hand-rolling

You wrote the loop to understand it. You do not have to keep it.

Once the loop holds no mystery, the hand-written version stops earning its keep — it is boilerplate you now have to maintain. The SDK's tool runner takes the same tools and runs the same cycle:

from anthropic import beta_tool

@beta_tool
def kb_search(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the paper corpus by keyword.

    Args:
        query: search terms.
    """
    return ...                       # schema generated from the signature

runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
    model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=16000,
    tools=[kb_search],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": goal}],
)
for message in runner:               # loop, execution and halting handled
    print(message)

The schema now comes from the type hints and the docstring, which is the same information in a place that cannot drift from the code. You keep per-turn control: inspect each message as it arrives, gate a call for approval, retry, or modify a result before it goes back.

What you lose is not control — it is the exception path. A helper that ends its loop on any turn where no client tool ran will exit silently on a pause_turn, handing you a truncated answer with no error. That is precisely the failure §2 warned about, relocated into someone else's code. Knowing the manual loop is what lets you recognize it.

Now build one. Exercise p1 in practice/: take the eighty lines above, point kb_search at a real corpus, and ask it a question whose answer is not in the weights.

Try thisWhat you should seeWhich idea
Print messages at every stepthe transcript growing by two rows per cycle§1 — context is the only state
Ask something answerable from memoryit answers without calling the tool — no tool_use at all§2 — the model chooses; you cannot make it call
Make execute raise on purposewith is_error, it adapts; without, the run dies§5 — failure is data
Return 5 000 lines from the toollater answers get worse, not better§5 — the flooding failure → ch. 04
Set max_steps=2 on a task needing fourthe bound fires — an agent that "didn't finish", not one that crashed§4 — the halt is yours

You can now say what crosses the wire on a tool call, where the loop lives, who owns the state, and what each stop_reason obliges you to do — and you can place all four build shapes on the harness × deployment grid. If any of those is still fuzzy, it is §2 and §3 that repay a second read.

Next: every one of those tool_result blocks stays in the transcript and is re-read on every subsequent step. Deciding what goes in there is not a detail — it is the main design problem of a working agent. That is chapter 04.
